description: İAFL Cosmos is a two-member student team from İstanbul Atatürk Fen Lisesi (Istanbul Atatürk Science High School), one of Türkiye's leading science high schools. Both of us code: one member drives the software, machine learning and data pipeline, while the other leads design, storytelling and presentation. We cover each other's gaps, so ideas move quickly from data to a working product and a clear story. We came to Space Apps to turn open NASA data into tools people can actually use.
summary:
Satellites have recorded active fires for more than 20 years, but the record comes from two instruments that cannot be compared directly. VIIRS has much smaller pixels than MODIS and reports many more hot spots for the same fires; in the Antalya–Muğla study area, about 6.6 times as many. Joining the two records creates a false jump in fire activity, and with MODIS nearing the end of its mission, the long-term record is at risk.

FireA Harmonizer is a web app built on NASA FIRMS data. Its core is FireA-v1, a neural network trained on 3.58 million detections from 15 fire regions, which converts VIIRS detections into MODIS-equivalent counts with uncertainty intervals. The app uses this to build a continuous monthly record from 2003 to today for any selected area, and turns it into a burning activity calendar with critical fire periods, unusual months, an anomaly map and an early-warning view.

Each area is checked against real MODIS where both sensors overlap. The result gives emergency teams, scientists and land managers a consistent long-term view of fire activity that can continue after MODIS ends.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) record the same fires differently: in our Antalya–Muğla study area, raw VIIRS reports a median of 6.6 times as many hot spots, so joining the records creates a false jump in 2012. FireA Harmonizer downloads NASA FIRMS data for any selected area. Our neural network FireA-v1, trained on 3.58 million detections from 15 fire regions, converts each VIIRS cluster into the number of detections MODIS would have reported. The app then builds one monthly record from 2003 to today: a burning activity calendar, the critical fire season, the busiest years and months, unusual months as probabilities, an anomaly map and a 48-hour early-warning view.

What benefits does it have?

The record stays consistent in MODIS units: the 6.6× gap drops to 0.91× before any local calibration. In regions the model never saw during training, it beat gradient boosting and a power law. In Antalya–Muğla (2012–2022, leaving out one year at a time), the median monthly error is 21.7% (24.8% for a constant ratio), yearly totals have a median error of 16.9% (3.7% with two VIIRS satellites), and 84.7% of real values fall inside the 80% interval. Users see fire seasons, unusual months and how certain each estimate is.

What is the intended impact?

Both MODIS satellites are near the end of their missions. The harmonized record lets the long-term fire record continue after them for emergency teams, scientists and land managers.

What tools did we use?

Python and TypeScript; FastAPI, PyTorch, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy and SciPy; React and Leaflet; NASA FIRMS API; Esri and OpenStreetMap maps. Training ran on a laptop CPU in about 30 minutes. We used Claude and ChatGPT during development (see AI_DISCLOSURE.md).

How is it creative?

Instead of a fixed ratio, we ask "What would MODIS have seen?" fire by fire, measure Aqua's orbit drift from the data and combine three VIIRS satellites.

What factors did we consider?

Honest uncertainty ("no detection" is never "no fire"), an independent test region, a server-side API key, English and Turkish, a colour-blind friendly palette and documented limitations.

More details, including methods, validation and limitations, are in the README of our GitHub repository.
